title: Two standards
hookLine: two banners: riches, honor, pride, or poverty, insults, humility

lines: A MAP OF HOW A LIFE SLIDES.
cards: Two camps on two great fields. Near Babylon, a banner held by the enemy of human nature, who sits on a throne of fire and smoke. Near Jerusalem, Christ's banner, and Christ stands in a lowly place.
That's the stage Ignatius of Loyola sets in the second week of his Spiritual Exercises. An old word for a banner carried into battle is a standard, so the meditation is called the two standards.
But Ignatius isn't painting a war movie. He's drawing a map of how a life slides, one small step at a time, toward one banner or the other.

teach.b: Under the first banner, Ignatius says, the tempter works in three steps. First, riches: the urge to have. Then honor: the wish to be admired for what you have.
Then pride: the swollen sense of being above others. From those three, he says, the tempter leads on to all the other vices. The first step doesn't look wicked.
Wanting things is ordinary. It's the ladder that worries him. Under the second banner, Christ sends his friends out with a plan that mirrors it.

First, poverty: at the very least poverty of spirit, a loose grip on things, and actual poverty if God calls someone there. Then a willingness to be overlooked, even insulted, instead of praised. Then humility.

teach.h: NO MAN CAN SERVE TWO MASTERS.
teach.b: Jesus puts the choice plainly in Matthew: "No man can serve two masters."

And Paul traces the second path in Christ himself, who "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant." No reputation: the second step, lived by the one who carries the banner.

This meditation can be misheard as a call to be miserable, or to go looking for insults. Ignatius is careful. The one praying asks to be received under Christ's banner, and to be given these things only if they serve God.
It's a check on direction, not a hunt for hardship. And it's honest about how pride usually gets in: not with a crash, but through a small, reasonable-looking first step.

how: In the Spiritual Exercises, the Two Standards is prayed during the second week and is followed by a colloquy asking to be received under Christ's standard.

o: Ignatius' meditation on Christ's banner and the tempter's banner

games.q: under the enemy's banner, Ignatius lists three steps. which comes first?
games.why: riches first, then honor, then pride. the first step looks ordinary, and that's why Ignatius watches it.

practice: See the two fields and the two banners lifting in the wind, then think back over the last day or two: where did you reach for more, want to be seen or praised, or slide toward feeling above someone, and where did you let go, let someone else have the credit, or take the lower seat?
Don't judge it; just see which way you leaned. If you pray, you can ask to stand under Christ's banner.

wordCard.voice: Two standards. Ignatius' meditation on two banners: riches, honor and pride under one; poverty, insults and humility under the other.

orig.note: Spanish, in Latin letters, Ignatius' own language: a flag or banner, the word behind the two standards.

carryVoice: Your line: under his banner. A loose grip, a lower seat, and no hunt for hardship. Until tomorrow.
